sources.citation: Lovestrand, Joseph. 2013. East Chadic B: Classification and description progress report. Journal of West African Languages 40(1): 105-130.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for jeu or any other language; the paper is taxonomic history + lexicostatistics. The only tone-term matches are bibliography titles (Fédry 1974 Dangaléat 'énigme tonale'; Roberts 2012 'The tone system of Mawa'). Confirms (2013) that no linguistic data for Jonkor Bourmataguil exist beyond Roberts' 1993 unpublished trip narrative.

sources.citation: Lovestrand, Joseph. 2012. Classification and description of the Chadic languages of the Guéra (East Chadic B). SIL Electronic Working Papers 2012-004. Dallas: SIL International. 59 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for any language: the phonology chapter (§4) covers consonant inventories, vowels and CV structures only, and Jonkor Bourmataguil is explicitly excluded from §4 (phonology), §4.2 (vowels) and §5 (pronouns) for lack of data. What it does state about jeu: (i) no linguistic data exist apart from Roberts' 1993 narrative of a trip to the homeland (Table 1 files jeu under 'wordlist' with Tamki, Mabire, Kujarge); (ii) Roberts observed that the language 'appears to have lost its bilabial plosive' (uses the labial fricative, like Dangla-group neighbours); (iii) speakers call…

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. (n.d., updated ms.). The Chadic languages: classification and language list. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); the open copy could not be downloaded when a reader tried
sources.note: Blench's running classification lists every Chadic ISO code with known sources and notes on unresearched languages; would confirm that no field data exist for jeu and may name the SIL Chad survey behind Ethnologue's location and dialect details.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2007. Endangered languages in Central Africa. In Brenzinger (ed.), Language Diversity Endangered, 163-178. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Second of Glottolog's three references; an endangerment survey table only (snippet seen), so it will not describe stress, but it is the most recent published mention and could cite a field source.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page jonk1238 'Jonkor Bourmataguil' (Hammarström et al.), with reference list and dialect tree
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Only three references (Jungraithmayr 1981 overview; Connell 2007 overview; Moseley 2010 atlas), every one rated Glottolog's most extensive description 'a wordlist or less'; subclassification comment cites Jungraithmayr 1981; two dialects Dougne and Musunye with no references of their own.

sources.citation: SIL Chad / Johnstone (1993)-era survey notes behind the Ethnologue 14th-ed. (2000) entry (population 1,500, villages Bourmataguil and Ader-Ader, dialects Dougne and Musunye, 'Karakir = cave-dwellers')
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The Ethnologue entry is the only place with first-hand sociolinguistic detail; the underlying survey report (if one exists in the SIL Chad archive) might contain a short wordlist. Not identified in any catalogue searched; sil.org search blocked.

sources.note: The only publication Glottolog ties to the language and the source of its Dangla-group placement; a 13-page family overview, so at most a listing and perhaps a note on Chadic prosody in general, but it is the sole item that could carry any first-hand remark. Lending copy on archive.org (leslanguesdansle0040unse) requires a borrow; Harvard/BnF hold print (ISBN 2222017203).

Originally centered in Bourmataguil village, now centered in Ader-Ader.. two villages the children still learn Jonkor Bourmataguil. Connell 2007 p.175 snippet: 'Jonkor Bourmataguil <1,500 Replaced by Chadic Arabic; may still..'. No phonological content anywhere.
